newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korea's Kim rules out compromise on labour bill.
newsitem.headline: S.Korea's Kim rules out compromise on labour bill.

text.p: South Korean President Kim Young-sam on Tuesday ruled out compromise over a controversial new labour bill, angering militant unions who vowed to step up strikes engulfing the economy.
At a news conference, Kim threw his weight behind the legislation, which shatters near-total job security by allowing worker layoffs, declaring "it is not an evil law".
Unions had demanded Kim use his traditional New Year press conference to announce the scrapping of the bill.

Hours after Kim's hardline comments, the head of the outlawed Korean Confederation of Trade Unions said he would bring out public sector unions to join stoppages that have idled shipbuilding yards and car plants.
"We have no choice but to intensify our strikes," Kwon Young-kil told reporters.
Subway drivers and workers at state-owned telecommunications giant Korea Telecom would join industrial action, Kwon said, without giving a timetable.

"Kim should have offered to talk over the issue," Kwon said. "But there was no offer of talks, let alone an apology." Separately, a union statement said construction and office workers would walk out.
Hospital workers and unionists at four big broadcasters joined the snowballing strikes on Tuesday intended to pressure the government into dropping the law.
The confederation said 217,000 workers were now idle, up from 190,000 on Monday.

Strikers represent just a fraction of South Korea's workforce of more than 10 million. But they are concentrated in huge industrial conglomerates, such as the Hyundai Group, which are the backbone of the export-led economy.
Kim offered no hint of compromise, saying the law was urgently needed to enhance South Korea's economic competitiveness and rescue a struggling economy saddled with high costs and low efficiency.
He ruled out a meeting with opposition parties to try to resolve the crisis.
"A country that cannot compete is bound to fall behind," Kim said.
Helping companies cut costs and boost sales would narrow South Korea's trade deficit, Kim said, pledging also to lower interest rates, land prices and transport costs.
"There have been a lot of misunderstandings among the Korean people about this new labour law. We have had the old one for 43 years and it hasn't changed," Kim said.

"Nobody will wear clothes from 43 years ago. We need a labour law that meets the standards of advanced countries. Both employers and workers might be disenchanted with the law but we all need to persevere."
Kim's tough stand sets the government more firmly on collision course with union leaders, who are camped out in the snow under plastic sheeting in the shadow of Seoul's gothic Myongdong Cathedral.
On Monday, state prosecutors summoned dozens of confederation leaders for questioning and repeated the order on Tuesday after being rebuffed.

Employers have threatened to sue union heads over production losses caused by the strikes, which erupted the day the new bill was rammed through parliament on December 26 with no debate and no opposition deputies present.
On Tuesday the government put total losses from the industrial unrest so far at 1.18 trillion won ($1.4 billion), including $244 million in lost export earnings.
The main opposition National Congress for New Politics condemned Kim's comments.
"He showed no responsibility or repentance over the economic crisis or the labour strikes. He has given up his responsibility to govern," a party statement said.

Some 15,000 nurses and orderlies at 24 hospitals resumed stoppages, leaving only emergency care. Around 8,000 workers at four broadcasters, including state-run Korea Broadcasting System, also walked out.
